Musicians think of breaking the fingers of Bo Ya <note>a legendary master of the zither whose skill aroused envy</note>; charioteers wish to shove aside the hands of Wang Liang <note>a famous charioteer of antiquity</note>. Why is this? It is because they wish to monopolize the reputation for excellence and skill, and loathe seeing others surpass themselves.

For this reason, the beauty from Wei was exquisitely gorgeous, yet Zheng Xiu <note>the jealous consort of King Huai of Chu who deceived the newcomer into covering her nose and then had it cut off</note> had her nose severed; Chao Wu was loyal and steadfast, yet Wu Ji <note>a corrupt minister of Chu who slandered Chao Wu</note> drove him into exile. The afflicted hunchback is intensely jealous, and the deformed cripple is full of flattery <note>allusions to figures in the Classic of Poetry representing petty or resentful courtiers</note>. Therefore, on damp ground in a hall, dust does not scatter; beneath a low roof, the wind cannot be blocked. Things standing directly in the rush of the gale cannot grow to maturity; the banks where water rushes in a torrent cannot maintain steep cliffs.

§. 34. When a man is perfectly satisfied with the state in which he is, or when he is absolutely free from all uneasiness, what will can remain to him but to continue in this state? Thus the wise Author of our being has placed in men the discomfort of hunger and thirst, and other natural desires, in order to excite and determine their wills toward their own preservation and the continuation of their species. It is better, says St. Paul (1 Cor. VII. 9.), to marry than to burn. So true is it that the present feeling of a small burning has more power over us than the attractions of greater pleasures considered at a distance.

§. 35. It is true that this is a maxim so firmly established—that it is the good and the greatest good which determines the will—that I am in no way surprised at having assumed it as indubitable. However, after a careful search, I feel forced to conclude that the good and the greatest good, though judged and recognized as such, does not determine the will at all; unless, coming to desire it in a manner proportioned to its excellence, this desire makes us uneasy because we are deprived of it. {D476} In the language of India: *Śrī Bhagavān Ekajaṭa Mahākalpa Tantra Rāja Nāma*. <note>The edition records variant spellings of "Tantra" in the Sanskrit title: *tanta* and *tantra*.</note> In the language of Tibet: *The Great King of Tantras, the Ritual Tantra of the Glorious Blessed One, the Single-Braided One*. <note>Ekajaṭa, "the one with a single braid of matted hair," is a fierce protector deity of the tantric tradition, best known in female form as Ekajaṭā.</note>

Homage to the Blessed One, the Single-Braided One!

Thus have I heard at one time. The Blessed One was dwelling at the summit of the Vajra Mountain, in the abode of <term>Alakāvatī</term> <gloss>the "Willow-Locked" realm, traditional abode of Vajrapāṇi</gloss>. He dwelt together with countless bodhisattvas, great beings: the bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the King of Terrifiers, the Lord of the Nāgas, the one with the faces of Sun and Moon, the Seal of Arrayed Wisdom, and others. They had gained mastery over the deeply hidden treasury of secret suchness. They were perfectly established in the <term>maṇḍalas</term> <gloss>sacred circles</gloss> of all the <term>tathāgatas</term> <gloss>"thus-gone ones," buddhas</gloss>. They abided in the manner of an ocean of seals: the families, the assemblies, the sacred pledges, and the great vows. They delighted in great bliss, more secret than the secret itself. They possessed the wisdom that arises from the union of unsurpassed method and wisdom. They were skilled at overcoming both the manifest and the latent afflictions of all beings.

Then the bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi rose from his seat, placed his right knee upon the ground, joined his palms together, and addressed the Blessed One with these words:

Vajra Lord, great Vajra,
Vajra King, Lord of all,
Father who gives birth to all the buddhas,
Speak to me of the wheel of great bliss.

You who clear away the dense darkness of the three realms of existence,
Yet do not remain in <term>nirvāṇa</term> <gloss>final peace beyond suffering</gloss>,
Great loving one who protects all embodied beings,
Guide, I pray you, teach the path.

By which method, when meditated upon
By one steadfast in intelligence and compassion,
Is the seal of the five bodies accomplished? <note>The "five bodies" (*kāya*) are the five dimensions of a buddha's being in tantric doctrine.</note>
Lord, I pray you, explain that here.

That which arises greatly from the vajra maṇḍala,
Taught in the great tantra of a hundred thousand verses,
The principal maṇḍala of the garland of the Single-Braided One:
Whatever is hidden, speak of it out of love.

Thus

## To the Benevolent Reader. Greetings.

<meta>An ornate woodcut initial letter I features floral and scrolling foliate designs.</meta>

SINCE friends request a copy of the sermon I delivered in public, and patrons command it, and since I cannot keep pace with everyone by copying it out by hand, I seek the assistance of the printing press to record it in a condensed form.

If it should fall into foreign hands, let them know: this is not the speech itself, but rather the *Idea* <note>original: "Idea"; concept or outline</note> of the speech, which I had written out at greater length. However, the *solemnity* of the day on which it was spoken reduced it to this *Epitome* <note>original: "Epitomen"; summary</note>. Yet it is read as it was *spoken, in the very words conceived*. It is not the *Confession* <note>original: "Confessio"; a formal statement of faith</note> which I approved in writing before the Venerable Ministry before liberty was granted to this profession; rather, it is a defense of the EXIT from BABYLON. I call it an EXODUS, and I foresee the *desert*: there are *serpents* in it, and many adversaries. But being secure in the *Columns; the Cloud* that covers, and the *fire* that shines, I strive toward the heavenly Canaan.

I point out the reasons for this *Exodus* through an *Epitome*, which I had explained more copiously in the *speech*. These reasons are not lacking in divine authority, having been demonstrated by so many orthodox writers.

It should have been spoken in the Roman <note>i.e., Latin</note> tongue, but it was explained in the vernacular so that the Germans might know the sense of my German <note>a play on the words "Germani" and "germanae," meaning "true" or "genuine"</note> faith, and indeed the constancy of my purpose.

You see, therefore, Benevolent Reader, what was spoken for the ears, because you seek it, is now to be read by the eyes, to which I entrust the secrets of my mind and your own soul. What was said BEFORE YOU, I would have said BEFORE GOD, to whom I prove the innermost parts of my heart in this profession. It is brief indeed, but it suffices for the candid, who prefer truth without loquacity and without pretense. You know, therefore, for what reason the press prints this IDEA: lest it weigh upon me, either by writing it many times or by denying it to many people. Let this be the idea: if either friends or enemies demand it, I will not deny either the speech, of which this is the idea, or the confession, of which this is the head. *For I can suffer, and indeed die, for the Truth, but I cannot remain silent.*

->Y. H. <note>An abbreviation for "Your Humble servant" or similar respectful closing.</note><-

->M. Ostrovvski.<-

Sitting in Siddhâsana, close the two ears with the two thumbs, the eyes with the index fingers, the nostrils with the middle fingers, the upper lip with the fore fingers, and the lower lip with the little fingers. Draw in the Prâna-Vâyu by Kâkî-mudrâ, (as in verse 86) and join it with the Apâna-Vâyu; contemplating the six chakras in their order, let the wise one awaken the sleeping serpent-Kundalinî, by repeating the mantra Hun (हुं), and Hansa (हंसः), and raising the Sakti (Force-kundali) with the jîva, place them at the thousand-petalled lotus. Being himself full of Sakti, being joined with the great Siva, let him think of the various pleasures and enjoyments. Let him contemplate on the union of Siva (spirit) and Sakti (force or energy) in this world. Being himself all bliss, let him realise that he is the Brahma. This Yoni-mudrâ is a great secret, difficult to be obtained even by the Devas. By once obtaining perfection in its practice, one enters verily into Samâdhi.

अथ योनिमुद्राफलकथनम् ।
ब्रह्महा भ्रूणहाचैव सुरापी गुरुतल्पगः ।
एतैः पापैर्न लिप्येत योनिमुद्रानिबन्धनात् ॥ ४३ ॥
यानि पापानि घोराणि उपपापानि यानि च ।
तानि सर्वाणि नश्यन्ति योनिमुद्रानिबन्धनात् ।
तस्मादभ्यसनं कुर्याद्यदि मुक्तिं समिच्छति ॥ ४४ ॥

*Its benefits.*

43—44. By the practice of this Mudrâ, one is never polluted by the sins of killing a Brâhmana, killing a fœtus, drinking liquor, or polluting the bed of the Preceptor. All the mortal sins and the venal sins are completely destroyed by the practice of this Mudrâ. Let him therefore practise it, if he wishes for emancipation.
